idiom_name: hand-written guard chain over a handler function pointer (or a seccomp filter tree / interposed shared library)
implementation_notes: C has no proxy construct, so the structure is written out: a gate is a struct holding a check function pointer and a pointer to the next handler, and the entry point calls the check and forwards only on success; the same shape appears as a chain of interposed function wrappers or, below the process, as seccomp filters, where further filters may be added and each is evaluated in order and can only narrow what the earlier ones allow. What replaces the classic structure: nothing in the language - a struct plus function pointers, or the loader's interposition of a guarded symbol, is the structure - so the classic form is exactly what you write, and it is justified whenever the guarded interface is C (a socket, an ioctl, a library handle) rather than a framework request pipeline. Keep one translation unit per gate and pass identity explicitly through a context struct that each gate validates before use.
pitfalls: A function-pointer chain is only complete if every entry point uses it: a second exported symbol or a direct handler call silently skips the gates, and the chain then documents security that is not there.
seccomp filter trees can only narrow - a later filter cannot grant what an earlier one denies - so filter order and the allow-list versus deny-list choice are security decisions, not style.
The identity context is shared by pointer and mutated in place; a gate that changes it and returns early leaks the change into the next request of a long-lived process.
